summary.title: Atmospheric pressure continuous flow methane oxidation to methanol and acetic acid using H 2 O 2 over Au-Fe catalyst
summary.authors: Anuradha V Jagtap, Pawan Kumar, Sharad Gupta, N Abharana, S N Jha, D Bhattacharyya, T G Ajithkumar, C P Vinod
summary.executive_summary: The direct partial oxidation of methane (POM) to methanol and acetic acid is a significant catalytic challenge due to the thermodynamic drive towards complete oxidation to CO2. This study presents a modified silica-supported bimetallic catalyst (AuFeHS) that achieves high-yield methane conversion under mild, atmospheric pressure conditions in a continuous flow reactor. The catalyst, synthesized via a modified deposition precipitation method, features atomic Fe clusters and small Au nanoparticles (1.3-3.0 nm) on a hydrophobic silica support. Characterization techniques including XPS, XANES, and HRTEM reveal that the synergy between Au and Fe is crucial, with Au stabilizing low-valent Fe species (Fe 3-δ+) that are active for methane activation. In batch experiments at 10 bar, the AuFeHS catalyst achieved a methanol yield of 1666 mmol/gFe+Au with 95% selectivity. When CO was co-fed, the selectivity switched to acetic acid, yielding 3403 µmol/gcat. In the continuous flow process at atmospheric pressure, the catalyst produced methanol with a yield of 224 mmol/gFe+Au over 4 hours, significantly outperforming previous high-pressure batch processes. The hydrophobic nature of the support was identified as critical for maintaining peroxide proximity to active sites and facilitating product desorption. Isotope labeling experiments confirmed that the methanol carbon originates from methane, not the support. This work demonstrates a viable pathway for the commercialization of methane-to-oxygenates technologies under benign conditions, highlighting the importance of bimetallic modulation and support hydrophobicity in stabilizing active catalytic species.

claims.description: AuFeHS catalyst achieves high-yield methane oxidation at atmospheric pressure.
Co-feeding CO switches selectivity to acetic acid.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
The direct partial oxidation of methane (POM) to methanol and acetic acid is a significant catalytic challenge due to the thermodynamic drive towards complete oxidation to CO2. This study presents a modified silica-supported bimetallic catalyst (AuFeHS) that achieves high-yield methane conversion under mild, atmospheric pressure conditions in a continuous flow reactor. The catalyst, synthesized via a modified deposition precipitation method, features atomic Fe clusters and small Au nanoparticles (1.3-3.0 nm) on a hydrophobic silica support. Characterization techniques including XPS, XANES, and HRTEM reveal that the synergy between Au and Fe is crucial, with Au stabilizing low-valent Fe species (Fe 3-δ+) that are active for methane activation. In batch experiments at 10 bar, the AuFeHS catalyst achieved a methanol yield of 1666 mmol/gFe+Au with 95% selectivity. When CO was co-fed, the selectivity switched to acetic acid, yielding 3403 µmol/gcat. In the continuous flow process at atmospheric pressure, the catalyst produced methanol with a yield of 224 mmol/gFe+Au over 4 hours, significantly outperforming previous high-pressure batch processes. The hydrophobic nature of the support was identified as critical for maintaining peroxide proximity to active sites and facilitating product desorption. Isotope labeling experiments confirmed that the methanol carbon originates from methane, not the support. This work demonstrates a viable pathway for the commercialization of methane-to-oxygenates technologies under benign conditions, highlighting the importance of bimetallic modulation and support hydrophobicity in stabilizing active catalytic species.

Research Context
Methane activation is difficult due to its non-polar tetrahedral structure. Partial oxidation to methanol is a 'holy grail' problem in catalysis. Previous methods often require harsh high-pressure and high-temperature conditions. Molecular oxygen yields are generally poor for commercialization. Hydrogen peroxide is a promising green oxidant for this conversion. Single-site catalysts have shown promise but often suffer from low selectivity. Continuous flow reports for POM to methanol are limited. Existing continuous flow processes often use high pressures.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aims to develop a catalyst for POM at atmospheric pressure. It hypothesizes that a bimetallic Au-Fe system on hydrophobic silica will enhance activity. The hypothesis includes that hydrophobicity helps peroxide stay near active sites. It predicts that co-feeding CO will switch selectivity to acetic acid. The goal is to surpass high-pressure batch process yields. The study seeks to stabilize active Fe species using Au. It aims to demonstrate continuous flow operation at mild conditions.

Methodological Details
A modified deposition precipitation method was used for catalyst synthesis. The support was hydrophobic silica (HS). The optimal catalyst had 0.46 wt% Fe and 0.23 wt% Au. Hydrophobicity was confirmed by a contact angle of 118 degrees. HRTEM showed Au nanoparticles of 1.3-3.0 nm. XPS identified Fe 3+ and low-valent Fe 3-δ+ species. XPS showed 85% Au 0 and 15% Au δ+ species. Batch reactions were conducted at 10 bar methane pressure. Continuous flow reactions were conducted at atmospheric pressure. H2O2 (15% w/v) was used as the oxidant. CO was co-fed to produce acetic acid. Isotope labeling with CD4 was used to verify product origin.

Procedures And Architectures
The catalyst was synthesized by depositing Fe onto hydrophobic silica. Au was added via a NaOH-assisted deposition process. Batch screening was performed at 10 bar and optimized temperature. Continuous flow used a fixed-bed reactor. The continuous flow process ran for up to 7 hours. Products were analyzed using GC and NMR. XANES and EXAFS were used to probe electronic structure. In-situ IR spectroscopy probed CO adsorption states.

Key Results
Batch methanol yield was 1666 mmol/gFe+Au with 95% selectivity. Batch acetic acid yield was 3403 µmol/gcat with CO co-feed. Continuous flow methanol yield was 224 mmol/gFe+Au. Continuous flow acetic acid yield was 648 µmol/gcat. The continuous flow rate was 0.42 molmethanol kgcatalyst -1 h -1. This rate is higher than previous O2-based continuous flow reports. FeHS alone produced 285 mmol/gFe in batch. AuHS alone produced 47.6 mmol/gAu in batch. No product was detected without methane, oxidant, or catalyst.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The synergy between Au and Fe is key to high activity. Au stabilizes low-valent Fe species necessary for methane activation. Hydrophobicity facilitates peroxide proximity and product desorption. Lewis acid sites help in C-H sigma complex formation. The mechanism involves CH3 and OH radical formation. This approach offers a path to commercial M2O technologies.

Contradictions And Limitations
The role of Na and Lewis acid sites is not fully explored. The study focuses on specific bimetallic compositions. Long-term stability in continuous flow is not extensively detailed. The mechanism for acetic acid formation is inferred from prior work.

Claims
AuFeHS catalyst achieves high-yield methane oxidation at atmospheric pressure. Yield of 224 mmol/gFe+Au in continuous flow. Selectivity of 95% for methanol in batch. Previous high-pressure processes had higher absolute yields in some cases. Enables milder, potentially more scalable industrial processes.
Co-feeding CO switches selectivity to acetic acid. Acetic acid yield of 3403 µmol/gcat in batch. Acetic acid yield of 648 µmol/gcat in flow. Methanol is still formed as a side product. Provides a route to higher-value acetic acid from methane.

Data And Code Availability
Supporting information is available via ChemRxiv.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Control experiments showed no product without reactants or catalyst. Isotope labeling confirmed methane origin of methanol. Comparison with SBA-15 support showed lower activity.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows HRTEM images and elemental mapping. Figure 2 shows XPS and XANES spectra. Figure 3 shows batch catalytic activity and selectivity. Figure 4 shows continuous flow results. Table S6 compares literature values.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a high-yield Au-Fe catalyst for atmospheric POM. 2. The strongest evidence is the 224 mmol/gFe+Au yield in flow. 3. The future path is commercialization of methane-to-oxygenates tech.
